title: Do you speak Greek?
goal: Master the second verb group — the one whose stress always falls on the ending — and talk about the weather, languages, hunger, and thirst.
bekal: build the six forms of -άω / -ώ verbs
tell group A from group B by the stress
talk about the weather with subjectless verbs
say hungry and thirsty with a verb, not an adjective

dialogs.title: ΔΙΑΛΟΓΟΣ — Chatting with the neighbor
dialogs.intro: Kiria Maria, the downstairs neighbor, stops Ana on the stairs. Notice that every verb in this dialog is stressed on the **last** syllable — that is the badge of the second group.

lines.speaker: Κ. Μαρία:
lines.id: Good evening, dear. Do you speak Greek?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: A little. I ask a lot and answer a little!
lines.literal: I-speak — little. I-ask — much — and — I-answer — little!

lines.speaker: Κ. Μαρία:
lines.id: That's how we all start. Where are you from?
lines.literal: so — we-start — all. from — where — you-are?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: From Indonesia. There we speak Indonesian.
lines.literal: from — the — Indonesia. there — we-speak — Indonesian (language).

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Very hot, all year round. Here the winter is cold.
lines.literal: much (f) — heat, all — the — year. here — the — winter — it-is — cold.

lines.speaker: Κ. Μαρία:
lines.id: Today it's cold and raining a little.
lines.literal: today — it-makes — cold — and — it-rains — little.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: I love the sun, not the rain!
lines.literal: I-love — the — sun, not — the — rain!

lines.speaker: Κ. Μαρία:
lines.id: Me too, dear. Do you need anything?
lines.literal: and — I, child — my. you-ask-for — something?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: How do you say "potato" in Greek?

lines.speaker: Κ. Μαρία:
lines.id: Patata! That one you already know.

notes: **Greek has two verb groups, and the stress tells them apart.** Group A is stressed on the stem: μ**έ**νω, δουλ**έ**ω, δι**α**βάζω. Group B is stressed on the ending: μιλ**ά**ω, ρωτ**ά**ω, αγαπ**ά**ω. Once you hear the stress at the end, you know which endings to use.

**Group B has two faces, both correct**: μιλ**άω** and μιλ**ώ**, μιλ**άει** and μιλ**ά**, μιλ**άνε** and μιλ**ούν**. The -άω forms are more everyday; the -ώ forms are a bit neater and more common in writing. ⚠️ Pick one and stick with it; don't mix them in one sentence.

**Group B is small, but full of very common words**: μιλάω (speak), ρωτάω (ask), απαντάω (answer), αγαπάω (love), ζητάω (ask for), περνάω (pass, spend time), ξεκινάω (start), βοηθάω (help), πεινάω (be hungry), διψάω (be thirsty), σταματάω (stop), κολυμπάω (swim).

⚠️ **"Hungry" and "thirsty" are VERBS in Greek, not adjectives.** *Πεινάω* is literally "I hunger", *Διψάω* "I thirst". Translating straight from English as *Είμαι πεινασμένος* is understandable, but sounds like announcing a medical condition. The natural way: **Πεινάω** and **Διψάω**, one word.

**Weather uses verbs with no real subject.** *Κάνει ζέστη* is literally "it makes heat" — who "it" is never gets explained, just like the "it" in English *it's raining*. Common ones: **κάνει ζέστη / κρύο** (it's hot / cold), **βρέχει** (it's raining), **χιονίζει** (it's snowing), **φυσάει** (it's windy), **έχει ήλιο** (it's sunny), **έχει συννεφιά** (it's cloudy).

⚠️ **Πολύς changes; πολύ doesn't.** As "very" it stays **πολύ**: *πολύ καλός*. As "much / many" before a noun it agrees in gender: **πολύς** καφές, **πολλή** ζέστη, **πολύ** νερό, **πολλοί** άνθρωποι, **πολλές** μέρες, **πολλά** παιδιά. It gets two λ when it changes.

**Language names are always neuter plural and start with a lowercase letter**: ελληνικά, αγγλικά, ινδονησιακά, γαλλικά, γερμανικά, ισπανικά, αραβικά, κινέζικα. For "in …" use **στα**: *στα ελληνικά*, *στα αγγλικά*.
**Πώς λέμε … στα ελληνικά;** is the most useful sentence you can take to Greece. An equally common variant: *Πώς το λένε αυτό;* — "What's this called?", while pointing.

grammars.title: Group B: verbs stressed on the ending
body: Compare the two columns line by line. Only the endings differ — and where the stress falls.
after: Notice that the **εσύ** and **εσείς** forms have only one shape: μιλάς and μιλάτε. So only three lines really branch.

⚠️ There is a second, smaller group B that uses only the short forms: **μπορώ** (can), **οδηγώ** (drive), **τηλεφωνώ** (phone), **ζω** (live). Endings: -ώ, -είς, -εί, -ούμε, -είτε, -ούν. *Μπορώ, μπορείς, μπορεί, μπορούμε, μπορείτε, μπορούν.* You'll use it all through the next unit.

grammars.title: Weather and seasons
body: All weather verbs are used only in the "he/she/it" form and never have a named subject.
after: **Seasons:** η άνοιξη (*AH-nee-ksee*) spring · το καλοκαίρι (*kah-loh-KEH-ree*) summer · το φθινόπωρο (*fthee-NOH-poh-roh*) autumn · ο χειμώνας (*khee-MOH-nahs*) winter. Καλοκαίρι literally means "good weather" — an honest name for a Greek summer.
⚠️ A Greek summer can hit forty degrees Celsius, and winter in the north drops below zero. For newcomers from the tropics, **ο χειμώνας** is the real surprise — not **το καλοκαίρι**.

sections.title: The most common group B verbs

blocks.title: Περνάω καλά — a phrase to take home
items: **Περνάω καλά** = "I'm having a good time", literally "I pass well". *Πέρασα πολύ καλά!* — I had a great time! This is the standard answer to questions about a holiday, a party, or the weekend.
**Καλά περάσατε;** — "Did you have a good time?" You'll hear it every time you come back from anywhere.
⚠️ **Αγαπάω is used more sparingly than English *love*.** It's for people, countries, and big things. For everyday "like" — food, films, music — Greeks use **μου αρέσει**, fully unpacked in unit 17.

**Πεινάω** and **διψάω** are the first two words that should come out without thinking when you travel. Add **Κουράστηκα** (*koo-RAH-stee-kah*, "I'm tired") and you have the three basic human complaints.
